posts.title: Leadership needs no title
posts.excerpt: Some of the best leaders I have worked with did not have "manager" in their job title.
paragraphs: Some of the best leaders I have worked with did not have "manager" in their job title.
The receptionist who knew every regular customer by name.
The driver who called ahead when he was running late.
The junior officer who quietly trained every new hire.
Nobody appointed them.
People simply followed their example.

Here's the truth:
A title gives you authority. Only your conduct gives you influence.
You lead without the title when you take ownership of problems that are not "your department".
When you help a colleague without being asked.
When you speak up for the customer in a meeting where no one else does.
Promotions often recognise leadership that was already there.
You do not have to wait for permission to start.
Where can you lead this week, without waiting for a title?

posts.title: What you celebrate, grows
posts.excerpt: It's Friday, a good day to ask a simple question: What did we celebrate this week?
paragraphs: It's Friday, a good day to ask a simple question:
What did we celebrate this week?
Many teams only celebrate the big numbers.
The record sale.
The new contract.
The target hit.
Those matter.
But if that is all you applaud, people learn that only results count, however they were achieved.

Here's the truth:
What you celebrate, grows.
Celebrate the staff member who calmed an angry customer.
Celebrate the person who raised a problem early.
Celebrate the colleague who helped someone else finish on time.
Celebrate honesty, ownership and care, not just the scoreboard.
Your team is always watching what earns your attention.
Make sure it is the behaviour you want to see again on Monday.
Who on your team deserves a specific "thank you" before the weekend?

posts.title: Ask how they want to be led
posts.excerpt: Most leaders lead people the way they themselves like to be led.
paragraphs: Most leaders lead people the way they themselves like to be led.
It feels natural.
It is not always effective.
One person wants detailed instructions.
Another wants the goal and the freedom to figure it out.
One wants praise in public.
Another would rather hear "well done" quietly, one-on-one.

Here's the truth:
You don't have to guess. You can ask.
"How do you like to receive feedback?"
"What helps you do your best work?"
"What should I stop doing that gets in your way?"
These questions take ten minutes.
The answers can save you months of frustration on both sides.
Great leadership is not one style applied to everyone.
It is paying attention to the person in front of you.
When last did you ask someone on your team how they want to be led?

posts.title: Lead yourself first
posts.excerpt: Before you lead a team, a department or a business, you lead one person.
paragraphs: Before you lead a team, a department or a business, you lead one person.
Yourself.
How you manage your time.
How you handle pressure.
How you speak when things go wrong.

Here's the truth:
You cannot take your team further than you have taken yourself.
Your people do not only listen to your instructions.
They watch your habits.
If you arrive late, deadlines become suggestions.
If you shout under pressure, they learn to hide problems.
If you keep learning, they start learning too.
Self-leadership is not glamorous.
It is the quiet work of keeping your own promises before you ask others to keep theirs.
Over the next six weeks, I'll share one leadership lesson a day, all the way to the end of the year.
We start here, with the person in the mirror.
What is one habit you want to lead yourself on before the year ends?
